# Industrial Heat and Steam {#sec-industrial-heat}

## What this service covers

Many industrial processes need heat: to warm, cook, dry, evaporate, or distill a material. Most sites raise that heat in a central system, usually a boiler that makes steam, and pipe it to the process. CIMS calls this the **steam** service. It covers steam, hot water, thermal oil (an oil heated and pumped around a site to carry heat), and direct heat from a separate heater, whenever a site's heat system supplies it to a process.

CIMS splits industrial heat into three bands by the temperature the process needs. The band matters because it decides which technologies can do the job:

| Band | Temperature | Typical uses |
|:-----|:-----------:|:-------------|
| Low | Below 150 °C | Hot water and low-pressure steam for washing, pasteurizing, bleaching, warming pulp stock, evaporating liquids, and drying at low temperature. |
| Medium | 150–400 °C | Higher-pressure steam, thermal oil, and direct heaters for distillation, digesters, stripping, melting polymers, pressing panels, and the heaters that feed refinery distillation. |
| High | Above 400 °C | Fired heaters and furnaces that stand apart from the equipment they serve, mainly refinery process heaters. |

: Industrial heat bands in CIMS {#tbl-heat-bands}

The 150 °C boundary is about where commercial heat pumps stop, so it marks the band in which they can compete. Above about 200 °C heat pumps fall away, leaving combustion, electric boilers and heaters, heat storage, and cogeneration. Natural Resources Canada reports industrial heat in different bands (below 200 °C, 200–700 °C, and above 700 °C), which don't line up with these.

The steam service doesn't cover heat released *inside* a sector's own process equipment. The heat inside a cement kiln, a blast furnace, a steam cracker's furnace, a lime kiln, or a glass furnace belongs to that sector's process step and its technologies.

Industrial heat makes up about two-thirds of the energy industry uses worldwide and roughly one-fifth of energy-related CO~2~ emissions. Across IEA member countries, 30–45 % of industrial heat demand is at low temperature [@iea-fop; @iea-renewables; @madeddu].

## Where heat sits in the model

Each industrial sector that raises steam has a **steam** service, and the sector's process technologies draw on it. Nine sectors have one: Biofuels, Chemicals, Iron and Steel, Light Industrial, Metal Smelting, Mining, Petroleum Crude, Petroleum Refining, and Pulp and Paper. The same heat-supply technologies compete in every one, so this chapter lists them once.

Two other services supply direct heat from separate heaters. Petroleum Refining has a **direct heat** service for its fired process heaters, the only service in the high band, and the Natural Gas sector's gas-processing chain has a direct heat step for its heaters. Their technologies are listed in those sector chapters.

**Cogeneration** is not a service of its own. A combined heat and power (CHP) unit is one of the technologies that can supply a steam service, with electricity as a by-product; see @sec-cogen.

CIMS sets each sector's starting heat demand, by province, by calibrating to Statistics Canada and Natural Resources Canada's Comprehensive Energy Use Database (CEUD), Environment and Climate Change Canada's National Inventory Report (NIR), and the U.S. Energy Information Administration's Manufacturing Energy Consumption Survey (MECS). The CEUD doesn't report process heat by temperature, but it shows that steam systems, boilers, and process heating account for most of the fossil fuel used in Canadian manufacturing [@nrcan-ceud].

## Heat uses by sector

@tbl-heat-end-uses lists typical heat uses and their temperatures in Canadian industry. Food and beverage processing, textiles, wood products, and light manufacturing aren't separate sectors in CIMS: Light Industrial covers them and splits its heat into its own end uses (see @sec-light-industrial).

| Sector | Typical heat uses | Range (°C) |
|:----|:---------|:-:|
| Pulp and paper | Evaporating black liquor, drying paper on steam-heated cylinders, heating digesters | 100–180 |
| Chemicals | Distillation reboilers, heating batch reactors, crystallization | 80–180 |
| Mining, and oil and gas | Heating produced water, regenerating glycol, heating remote sites, processing gas | 60–200 |
| Food and beverage | Pasteurizing, sterilizing, spray and tray drying, cleaning-in-place wash water | 60–200 |
| Textiles, leather, and laundry | Dye baths, drying, finishing | 60–160 |
| Wood products | Kiln drying lumber, pressing panels | 60–200 |
| Light manufacturing and assembly | Curing paint, washing parts | 50–180 |

: Typical industrial heat uses and temperatures {#tbl-heat-end-uses}

## Technologies

The technologies below compete in every steam service. Each one is tagged with the heat bands it can reach, so it competes only where its temperature suits the demand.

{{< include _technology-blocks/general/steam.md >}}

The main options differ in how they make heat and what they use to do it:

### Boilers

A boiler burns fuel to heat water into steam. Fuel-fired boilers burn natural gas, oil, by-product gases, hydrogen, or biomethane; solid-fuel boilers burn biomass, coal, or waste. Efficiency measures, such as recovering heat from the flue gas, let a boiler raise the same steam on less fuel. A boiler can also be fitted with carbon capture, or run on pure oxygen so its flue gas is nearly pure CO~2~ and easier to capture [@dea_2026_001].

### Industrial heat pumps

A heat pump moves heat from a cooler source, such as waste heat or outside air, to a hotter one, using electricity to do the work. Because it moves heat rather than making it, it can deliver several units of heat for each unit of electricity. Commercial industrial heat pumps reach about 165 °C, and units that reach 200 °C with new working fluids are being demonstrated [@arpagaus_2018_001; @zuhlsdorf]. Mechanical vapour recompression, an open-cycle heat pump that compresses the vapour from an evaporator to reuse its heat, is the most mature type, common in dairy, sugar, and pulp operations. Very-high-temperature heat pumps push further, delivering steam at up to about 280 °C.

### Electric boilers

Electric resistance and electrode boilers turn electricity into steam at close to 100 % efficiency. They cost less to buy than heat pumps and are the simplest replacement for a packaged gas boiler, which suits retrofits where first cost matters [@eccc-nir; @element-energy_2018_001]. Other electric heating methods, such as induction, infrared, microwave, and dielectric heating, serve specific drying, curing, and surface-heating jobs, and appear in the sector chapters where those jobs sit [@madeddu].

### Solar thermal

Flat-plate and evacuated-tube solar collectors supply heat up to about 100 °C. Concentrating collectors that focus sunlight along a line (parabolic troughs and linear Fresnel mirrors) reach 150–400 °C. @schoeneberger estimate that about half of global industrial heat demand falls within the range today's commercial solar thermal technologies can reach. In Canada, sunshine is strongest in the Prairies and the southern interior of British Columbia [@iea-renewables].

### Bioenergy

Biomass boilers, biogas, and renewable natural gas can replace fossil fuels at sites built around combustion. Biomass is the main on-site heat source in Canadian pulp and paper, and it matters in food processing near a supply of feedstock [@nrcan-bioheat]. Outside pulp and paper, most Canadian bioheat systems are between 50 kW and 5 MW. The 2023 update of CanmetENERGY's Canadian Bioheat Database finds that more than 90 % of catalogued commercial, institutional, and small industrial systems burn wood chips (about 45 %) or wood pellets (about 46 %) [@nrcan-bioheat-survey]. Wood chips lead in Quebec, Ontario, British Columbia, and Nova Scotia; pellets account for nearly all use in New Brunswick and the Northwest Territories. CIMS represents the limits of sustainable biomass supply through supply curves, not at the level of each boiler.

### Geothermal heat and recovered waste heat

Geothermal wells, and ground-source heat pumps, can supply heat from below ground. Every industrial site is also a source of low-grade waste heat, from compressors, condensers, flue gases, and warm effluents, that it usually lets go. Analyses by U.S. national laboratories estimate that recovered waste heat could in principle supply 20–50 % of industrial process heat [@ornl-waste]. Waste-heat recovery units, such as economizers and waste-heat boilers, compete in the steam service to put some of it back to use.

### Heat storage

Storing heat in pressurized hot water, molten salt, or solid materials lets a site make heat with electricity when power is cheap and use it later, or keep solar heat for when the sun isn't shining. Heat storage competes in the steam service alongside the other heat-supply technologies, charged either by electricity or by recovered heat [@iea-fop].

### Hydrogen

Burning hydrogen for low-temperature heat rarely competes with electricity: turning electricity into hydrogen and then burning it loses far more energy than using an electric boiler or heat pump directly. Hydrogen's value lies mainly in high-temperature heat and as a chemical feedstock [@thiel; @rissman]. Fuel-fired boilers and heaters can burn hydrogen where a sector's fuel blend supplies it.

## Existing equipment

CIMS estimates the existing boilers in each sector and heat band from CEUD and NIR data for the starting year. Existing units stay in service for their expected lifetimes and then need replacing; policies or other pressures can retire them sooner. Capital costs, how easily each option can be fitted to an existing site (see @sec-technology-competition), and sensitivity to electricity prices vary widely across these technologies.
